original_question: For integers n >= 0, consider the numbers 2^(2^n) + 1. Are there infinitely many composite numbers of this form?
target_in_paper: Open Problem 1 in the arXiv version of the paper (the same statement appears as Problem 2.1 in the published version): Are there infinitely many composite numbers of the form 2^(2^n) + 1?
correct_elements: Your draft already matches the paper’s official open problem essentially verbatim. It asks exactly about the infinitude of composite values among numbers of the form 2^(2^n) + 1, keeps the scope narrow, and does not drift into the neighboring question about prime numbers of the same form.
refined_question: Are there infinitely many nonnegative integers n such that 2^(2^n) + 1 is composite?
justification: The draft is targeting the paper’s standalone open problem, not its internal Diophantine-boundedness conjecture. In the section devoted to numbers of the form 2^(2^n) + 1, the author first states Conjecture 2.1 (called Hypothesis 1 in the arXiv text), then proves in Theorem 2.1 that this conjecture would imply that 2^(2^x) + 1 is composite for infinitely many integers x > 1, and then records the official question itself as Problem 2.1: whether there are infinitely many composite numbers of the form 2^(2^n) + 1. So the closest paper-faithful stand-alone refinement of your draft is simply to make the quantifier explicit: ask for infinitely many n >= 0 with 2^(2^n) + 1 composite. Theorem 2.1 is only a one-way implication, not an equivalence, so it should not replace the open problem.
